demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He remembers the sound more than anything else—the wet, splintering crack of the birch tree splitting wrong, followed by the scream that shouldn’t have been there. That was fourteen months ago. A cold Tuesday in early November, the sky that flat gray that makes everything look washed out. He was felling a marked birch on a steep slope near the river, a tree he’d read a dozen times before—lean, sound, no widow-makers. But the crown caught another tree on the way down, twisted the trunk, and sent a heavy limb cartwheeling sideways into the young seasonal worker who had wandered just inside the danger zone.

He was the first one there. The man’s leg was bent at an angle that made his stomach drop. Sawdust and blood. He yelled for the radio, tried to stop the bleeding with his own jacket, kept saying *“I’m sorry, I’m sorry”* over and over while the man’s face turned the color of wet cement. The helicopter came, the man lived, lost most of the function in his left leg. They said it wasn’t his fault—the kid had stepped past the exclusion tape. But he still hears the crack, the scream, the wet sound of the tourniquet tightening.

Now, every morning before dawn, he stands on his porch in the dark and runs through the day’s hazards in his head like a litany: escape routes, wind direction, crew positioning, second-by-second mental imagery of every tree’s fall path. The ritual used to take five minutes. Now it takes twenty. His wife, Marie, finds him still standing there with his coffee gone cold, staring at the treeline. She doesn’t say anything anymore. She just touches his shoulder and goes back inside.

At work, he refuses to run a saw. He tells his supervisor he’s getting too old for the chainsaw, that it’s time to train younger guys, but the truth is his hands tremble when he holds the throttle. He volunteers for mapping and inventory work instead, walking stand boundaries with a clipboard, measuring diameters, noting beetle kill. The men respect him, but they’ve noticed he flinches at the sound of a felling wedge being hammered. He keeps his distance during lunch. Eats alone on a stump, facing the direction from which no one can approach without him seeing.

At night, the dreams come in fragments: a branch, a shout, the smell of wet leaves and copper. Sometimes he sees the kid’s leg, sometimes his own leg, sometimes he is the one on the ground and no one comes. He wakes up gasping, drenched, and then lies still for an hour listening to Marie breathe, afraid that if he closes his eyes again he will go back to that slope.

He has stopped driving near the river. Takes the long way into town. Has not touched his own chainsaw, which sits in the garage under a tarp. The other day Marie asked if he wanted to sell it. He said no, but he couldn’t explain why. It would feel like abandoning something. Like giving up on the part of himself that knew how to work a tree cleanly, that took pride in a hinge cut so perfect the trunk would fall exactly where he aimed. That man is still there somewhere, but he feels distant now, like a photograph of someone he used to know.

The hardest part, he told Marie once, is that he can still do the job. He knows, intellectually, that it was an accident. He knows the kid made a mistake. But knowing doesn’t change the feeling that his hands are dangerous. And so he holds them still. He maps the forest, but he does not touch it.
